Rectangles and cubes

A dice, a gift box, a school garden, a classroom: rectangles and cubes are everywhere. In this chapter you draw oblique drawings and nets of cubes, work out the perimeter and area of rectangles and composite shapes, and find the surface area and volume of cubes.

11 LESSONS4 UNITS1 LAB
WHAT YOU WILL LEARN IN THIS CHAPTER
  • describe the properties of the cube and build models of cubes
  • draw an oblique drawing with the receding edges at 45° and shortened by half
  • recognise and draw nets of cubes
  • work out the perimeter and area of rectangles and composite shapes
  • work out the surface area and volume of cubes and convert units

UNIT 13 LESSONS

1The cube and its oblique drawing

A dice, a Rubik’s Cube, a sugar cube: they all have the same shape. A cube is bounded by 6 squares of the same size. It has 12 edges of the same length and 8 vertices (corners).

At each vertex three edges meet, and they are perpendicular to each other. Opposite faces are parallel. You can build a solid model from modelling clay or wood, and a skeleton model from 12 drinking straws and 8 balls of modelling clay.

To show a cube on paper so that it looks three-dimensional, you make an oblique drawing. The front face is drawn at its true size. The edges that go towards the back are drawn slanting at an angle of 45° and only half as long. Edges that you could not really see are drawn dashed.

KEY POINT · CUBE AND OBLIQUE DRAWING

Cube: 6 square faces of the same size, 12 edges of the same length, 8 vertices.

Oblique drawing (receding edges at 45°, half length): 1. Front face as a square at true size. 2. Edges going to the back at an angle of 45° and half as long. 3. Complete the back face. 4. Hidden edges dashed.

On squared paper: the diagonal of a square runs at exactly 45°. But make sure you use half the length.

Labelling: at the bottom is the base ABCD, above it the top face EFGH, with E above A, F above B, G above C and H above D.

INTERACTIVE · OBLIQUE DRAWING

A cube has three edges a, b and c of the same length. Set them to the same value. The edge b going to the back appears half as long and slanting.

EXAMPLE 1 · MAKING AN OBLIQUE DRAWING

Draw the oblique drawing of a cube with an edge length of 4 cm.

Front face: a square with a side length of 4 cm. At three of its corners, draw an edge of 2 cm towards the back at an angle of 45°. Join the end points to make the back square. The three edges that meet at the back bottom left corner are hidden.

Front square 4 cm, slanting edges 2 cm, three edges dashed.

EXAMPLE 2 · A SKELETON MODEL

For a skeleton model made of wire, a cube has edges 5 cm long. How much wire do you need?

A cube has 12 edges of the same length: $12 \times 5\text{ cm} = 60\text{ cm}$.

You need 60 cm of wire.

EXERCISES

Draw the oblique drawing of a cube with an edge length of a) 3 cm   b) 5 cm.

a) Front square 3 cm, slanting edges 1.5 cm. b) Front square 5 cm, slanting edges 2.5 cm. In each case three hidden edges dashed.

How many faces, edges and vertices does a cube have? How many edges meet at a vertex?

6 faces, 12 edges, 8 vertices. At each vertex 3 edges meet.

Ben wants to build a skeleton model of a cube with an edge length of 8 cm. He has 1 m of wire. Is that enough?

$12 \times 8\text{ cm} = 96\text{ cm}$. 1 m is 100 cm. It is enough, and 4 cm are left over.

A cube has the base ABCD and the top face EFGH (E above A, F above B, …). Which edges are parallel to AB? Which edges meet AB and are perpendicular to it?

Parallel: DC, EF and HG. Perpendicular and meeting AB: AD, AE, BC and BF.

A big cube is built from 27 small cubes, 3 by 3 by 3. It is painted red on the outside. How many small cubes have 3, 2, 1 or no red faces at all?

Think of the vertices, edges and faces of the big cube.

3 red faces: the 8 corner cubes. 2 red faces: one on each of the 12 edges, so 12. 1 red face: the middle one on each of the 6 faces, so 6. None: the one cube in the middle. Check: $8 + 12 + 6 + 1 = 27$.

TEST YOURSELF!

How many edges does a cube have?

12: four at the bottom, four at the top, four upright.

How long do you draw an edge of 6 cm that goes towards the back in an oblique drawing?

Half as long: 3 cm.

All the edges of a cube are 84 cm long together. How long is one edge?

$84\text{ cm} \div 12 = 7\text{ cm}$

UNIT 22 LESSONS

2Nets of cubes

If you cut a cube-shaped box open along some of its edges and fold it out flat, you get a net of 6 squares. The other way round, you can fold a cube from a net. But not every arrangement of 6 squares can be folded into a cube.

A net of a cube consists of 6 squares that are joined along whole edges. When you fold it, no square may end up on top of another. There are exactly 11 different nets of a cube. Nets that are turned or flipped over do not count twice.

You can see on the net which faces of the cube are opposite each other: two squares that share an edge are never opposite. With three squares in a row, the first and the third are opposite.

KEY POINT · NETS OF CUBES

A net of a cube consists of 6 squares that are joined along edges and can be folded into a cube. There are exactly 11 different ones.

Squares that share an edge are never opposite. In a row of three squares, the two outer ones are opposite.

Never a net: a block of 2 by 2 squares, and a row of 5 squares.

Dice: the numbers of spots on opposite faces always add up to 7.

INTERACTIVE · IS IT A NET OF A CUBE?

Tap six squares. Can the shape be folded into a cube? How many of the 11 nets of a cube can you find?

EXAMPLE 3 · FIVE IN A ROW

Five squares lie in a row, the sixth above them. Is that a net of a cube?

If you fold the row round the cube, you are back at the start after four squares. The fifth square then lies on top of the first.

Not a net of a cube.

EXAMPLE 4 · WHAT IS OPPOSITE?

In the cross-shaped net, four squares lie in a row, one above and one below. Which faces are opposite each other?

In the row of four, the first and the third are opposite, and so are the second and the fourth. The square at the top and the one at the bottom become the lid and the base.

Three pairs: the 1st and 3rd and the 2nd and 4th square of the row, top and bottom.

EXERCISES

Draw the cross-shaped net of a cube with an edge length of 3 cm on squared paper, add glue tabs, cut it out and fold it into a cube.

The net is 4 squares, that is 12 cm, long and 3 squares, that is 9 cm, wide. The glue tabs go on the edges that are still open when you fold it.

Draw three different nets of a cube. Check them in the interactive box above.

For example the cross, the staircase (always two squares, moved along) and a row of four with one square at the top left and one at the bottom right.

In the cross-shaped net there is a 1 on the square in the middle of the cross. Which number belongs on the opposite square if the cube is to be a dice? Which square is that?

Opposite the 1 is the 6. That is the square two places further along in the row of four, so at the end of the long arm.

How many edges have to be glued together when you fold a net of a cube?

A cube has 12 edges. How many of them are already joined in the net?

In the net, 6 squares are joined along 5 edges. So 7 of the cube’s 12 edges are still missing: you need 7 glue tabs.

Find all 11 nets of a cube. Sort them by their longest row of squares: 4, 3 or 2.

With a row of four there are 6 nets, with a longest row of 3 squares 4 nets, and with rows of at most 2 squares only 1 net, the staircase. Together 11.

TEST YOURSELF!

How many different nets of a cube are there?

Exactly 11.

On a dice the 2 is on top. Which number is at the bottom?

Opposite faces add up to 7: $7 - 2 = 5$.

Which shape is a net of a cube?

The cross is a net of a cube. In the row of six and in the block, squares end up on top of each other when you fold them.

UNIT 33 LESSONS

3Perimeter and area

The school garden is a rectangle, 12 m long and 8 m wide. For the fence you need the perimeter: $12 + 8 + 12 + 8 = 40$ m. For the lawn you need the area: $12 \times 8 = 96$ square metres.

The perimeter $P$ of a shape is the length of its edge, that is the sum of all its side lengths. The area $A$ says how many unit squares fit into the shape. A rectangle 4 cm long and 3 cm wide contains 3 rows of 4 squares with a side length of 1 cm each, so $4 \times 3 = 12$ square centimetres (cm²).

For units of area the conversion factor is 100, because a square with a side length of 1 dm contains $10 \times 10 = 100$ squares with a side length of 1 cm. You can split shapes made of rectangles into parts, or complete them to make one big rectangle.

KEY POINT · RECTANGLE AND SQUARE

Rectangle with the sides $a$ and $b$: $P = 2 \times a + 2 \times b$  ·  $A = a \times b$

Square with the side $a$: $P = 4 \times a$  ·  $A = a \times a$

Units of area: 1 cm² = 100 mm² · 1 dm² = 100 cm² · 1 m² = 100 dm² · 1 a = 100 m² · 1 ha = 100 a · 1 km² = 100 ha

That is how big it is: 1 cm² is about a fingernail, 1 m² a square with a side length of 1 m, 1 a (an are) a square with a side length of 10 m, 1 ha (a hectare) a square with a side length of 100 m, a little bigger than a football pitch.

The same units: before multiplying, convert all the lengths into the same unit.

INTERACTIVE · RECTANGLES AND COMPOSITE SHAPES

Drag the corner. Under “Composite figure” you see how to split up or complete a shape.

INTERACTIVE · UNITS OF AREA

For areas, every step of the staircase is 100.

EXAMPLE 5 · AN L-SHAPED ROOM

A room is a square with a side length of 6 m, with a piece of 3 m by 2 m missing in one corner. How big is the floor area?

Completing: $6 \times 6 - 3 \times 2 = 36 - 6 = 30$. Or splitting: one rectangle $6 \times 4 = 24$ and one $3 \times 2 = 6$, together 30.

The floor area is 30 m².

EXAMPLE 6 · CONVERTING

Convert: a) 3 m² into dm²   b) 450 cm² into dm²   c) 2 ha into m²

a) $3 \times 100$   b) $450 \div 100$   c) $2 \times 100 \times 100$

a) 300 dm²   b) 4.5 dm²   c) 20,000 m²

EXERCISES

Work out the perimeter and the area: a) rectangle 8 cm by 5 cm   b) square with a side length of 7 m   c) rectangle 2 m by 45 cm

a) $P = 26$ cm, $A = 40$ cm²   b) $P = 28$ m, $A = 49$ m²   c) In cm: 200 cm by 45 cm, $P = 490$ cm = 4.9 m, $A = 9{,}000$ cm² = 90 dm²

a) 500 mm²   b) 3 m²   c) 250 dm²   d) 400 a

A rectangle has an area of 48 cm² and is 8 cm long. How wide is it? What is its perimeter?

$48 \div 8 = 6$, so it is 6 cm wide. $P = 2 \times 8 + 2 \times 6 = 28$ cm.

A room is 5 m long and 4 m wide. Carpet costs €15 per m². What does the carpet cost? A skirting board goes all the way round, except at the door, which is 1 m wide. How many metres of skirting board do you need?

$A = 20$ m², the carpet costs $20 \times 15 = 300$, so €300. Perimeter $2 \times 5 + 2 \times 4 = 18$ m, without the door 17 m of skirting board.

Find all the rectangles with a perimeter of 24 cm whose side lengths are whole centimetres. Which one has the biggest area?

Length and width together make half the perimeter.

Length plus width is 12 cm: 1 and 11 (11 cm²), 2 and 10 (20 cm²), 3 and 9 (27 cm²), 4 and 8 (32 cm²), 5 and 7 (35 cm²), 6 and 6 (36 cm²). The square has the biggest area.

TEST YOURSELF!

What is the area of a rectangle 9 cm long and 6 cm wide?

$9 \times 6 = 54$ cm²

What is the perimeter of a square with a side length of 12 m?

$4 \times 12 = 48$ m

How many cm² are 1 dm²?

$10 \times 10 = 100$

UNIT 43 LESSONS

4Surface area and volume of the cube

A present is in a cube-shaped box with an edge length of 10 cm. What is the least amount of paper you need to wrap it? The box has 6 faces of $10 \times 10 = 100$ cm² each, together 600 cm². And how much fits inside? $10 \times 10 \times 10 = 1{,}000$ small cubes with an edge length of 1 cm, so 1,000 cm³. That is exactly 1 litre.

The surface area $S$ of a cube is the area of its net: 6 squares of the same size. The volume $V$ says how many unit cubes fit inside: $a$ cubes in a row, $a$ rows in a layer, $a$ layers on top of each other.

For units of volume the conversion factor is 1,000, because 1,000 cubes with an edge length of 1 cm fit into a cube with an edge length of 1 dm: $10 \times 10 \times 10 = 1{,}000$. Liquids are measured in litres: 1 dm³ is 1 litre.

KEY POINT · SURFACE AREA AND VOLUME OF THE CUBE

Cube with the edge length $a$:   $S = 6 \times a \times a$  ·  $V = a \times a \times a$

Units of volume: 1 cm³ = 1,000 mm³ · 1 dm³ = 1,000 cm³ · 1 m³ = 1,000 dm³

Units of capacity: 1 dm³ = 1 l  ·  1 cm³ = 1 ml

Cubed: $a \times a \times a$ is also written $a^3$. That is why cm³ is called a cubic centimetre, from the Latin “cubus”, cube.

Double the edge: then the cube needs 4 times as much paper, but 8 times as much fits inside.

INTERACTIVE · VOLUME AND SURFACE AREA

Set all three edges to the same value; then the solid is a cube. Count the unit cubes layer by layer.

INTERACTIVE · SOLIDS MADE OF CUBES

A building made of cubes with an edge length of 1 cm. Tap a cell in the building plan to stack one more cube there.

EXAMPLE 7 · A CUBE WITH A 5 CM EDGE

Work out the surface area and the volume of a cube with an edge length of 5 cm.

$S = 6 \times 5 \times 5 = 6 \times 25 = 150$ and $V = 5 \times 5 \times 5 = 125$.

$S = 150$ cm², $V = 125$ cm³

EXAMPLE 8 · A CUBE-SHAPED AQUARIUM

A cube-shaped aquarium has an edge length of 40 cm on the inside. How many litres of water fit into it?

40 cm = 4 dm. $V = 4 \times 4 \times 4 = 64$ dm³.

64 litres fit into it.

EXERCISES

Work out the surface area and the volume of a cube with an edge length of a) 2 cm   b) 6 cm   c) 10 dm

a) 24 cm², 8 cm³   b) 216 cm², 216 cm³   c) 600 dm², 1,000 dm³

Convert: a) 3 dm³ into cm³   b) 5,000 cm³ into litres   c) 2 m³ into dm³   d) 750 ml into litres

a) 3,000 cm³   b) 5 dm³ = 5 l   c) 2,000 dm³   d) 0.75 l

A cube has a volume of 64 cm³. How long is one edge? What is its surface area?

$4 \times 4 \times 4 = 64$, so the edge is 4 cm long. $S = 6 \times 16 = 96$ cm².

A staircase is made of cubes with an edge length of 1 cm, all in one row: 4 cubes at the bottom, 3 on top of them, then 2 and 1 at the very top, all lined up on the left. What is its volume?

$4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 10$ cubes, so 10 cm³.

Packaging: What happens to the surface area and the volume if you double the edge length of a cube? Compare a = 2 cm and a = 4 cm. What does that mean for packaging?

a = 2 cm: $S = 24$ cm², $V = 8$ cm³. a = 4 cm: $S = 96$ cm², $V = 64$ cm³. The surface area becomes 4 times as big, the volume 8 times. A big pack needs less material for the same contents than lots of small ones.

TEST YOURSELF!

What is the volume of a cube with an edge length of 3 cm?

$3 \times 3 \times 3 = 27$ cm³

What is the surface area of this cube?

$6 \times 3 \times 3 = 54$ cm²

How many litres fit into a cube with an edge length of 1 m?

$10 \times 10 \times 10 = 1{,}000$ dm³ = 1,000 l

REVIEW · DEEPEN · CONNECT

Picture frame: A picture is 30 cm wide and 20 cm high. How long is the frame strip all the way round? How big is the glass in front of it?

$P = 2 \times 30 + 2 \times 20 = 100$ cm = 1 m. $A = 30 \times 20 = 600$ cm².

From net to cube: A net of a cube has squares with a side length of 5 cm. How much paper does it need without tabs? How much fits into the folded cube?

Paper: $6 \times 25 = 150$ cm². Volume: $5 \times 5 \times 5 = 125$ cm³.

A football pitch: A football pitch is 105 m long and 68 m wide. Is it bigger than a hectare?

$105 \times 68 = 7{,}140$ m². A hectare is 10,000 m². So the pitch is smaller, about 0.7 ha.

Cubes side by side: Three cubes with an edge length of 1 cm lie in a row. What is the surface area of the whole solid? And if you lay them out in an L?

Three separate cubes have $3 \times 6 = 18$ faces. Where two cubes touch, two faces disappear.

In the row the cubes touch in 2 places: $18 - 2 \times 2 = 14$ cm². In the L they also touch in 2 places: also 14 cm².

EXCURSIONHISTORY

How sugar became a cube

Sugar cubes have not been around for very long. In the past you bought sugar as a big, hard sugarloaf and broke pieces off it with a hammer and sugar nips. In the Moravian town of Datschitz, today Dačice in the Czech Republic, the Swiss Jakob Christoph Rad ran a sugar factory. The story goes that his wife Juliana hurt her finger while breaking up a sugarloaf.

Rad then developed a press that formed the sugar into small cubes of the same size. On 23 January 1843 he was granted a patent for it. The first cubes were sold as “tea sugar” in packets of half a kilogram.

Try it yourself: A cube-shaped tin has an edge length of 10 cm. How many sugar cubes with an edge length of 2 cm fit into it if you stack them neatly?

In each direction $10 \div 2 = 5$ cubes fit, so $5 \times 5 \times 5 = 125$ sugar cubes. Check with the volume: $1{,}000\text{ cm}^3 \div 8\text{ cm}^3 = 125$.

Sources: Goethe-Institut, “Der Würfelzucker” (goethe.de); town of Dačice, “World primacy” (dacice.cz): patent of 23 January 1843.

CUBE

6 squares of the same size, 12 edges of the same length, 8 vertices

Skeleton model with 5 cm: $12 \times 5 = 60$ cm of wire

OBLIQUE DRAWING

Front face at true size, towards the back 45° and half as long, hidden edges dashed

angle 45°, half length

NETS OF CUBES

6 squares, 11 different nets, neighbours are never opposite

Dice: opposite faces add up to 7

RECTANGLE

$P = 2 \times a + 2 \times b$, $A = a \times b$; units of area: conversion factor 100

$8\text{ cm} \times 5\text{ cm}$: $P = 26$ cm, $A = 40$ cm²

CALCULATING WITH CUBES

$S = 6 \times a \times a$, $V = a \times a \times a$; units of volume: 1,000; 1 dm³ = 1 l

$a = 5$ cm: $S = 150$ cm², $V = 125$ cm³
